blocks.prompt: Three Horns and a Shield of Bone
blocks.text: Triceratops did not have sharp teeth for meat. At the front of its mouth was a beak, hooked and curved like a parrot's beak. It used the beak to snip off tough plants. Behind the beak were rows and rows of teeth for cutting them up. Triceratops was heavy. It weighed more than an elephant. It walked on four thick legs and could not run fast. But it did not need to run. Its two long horns pointed forward, out over its eyes. Its shield of bone covered its neck. A Triceratops was a hard animal to bite.

blocks.prompt: The Head That Was Mostly Face
blocks.text: Triceratops had one of the biggest heads of any animal that has ever walked on land. Its skull could be eight feet long, about a third of the whole animal. Very little of that head was brain. Most of it was beak, horn, and bone. At the front was a beak, hooked and sharp like a parrot's. Triceratops used it to snip off branches and tough leaves. Behind the beak sat something stranger. Its teeth were packed into tall columns, stacked one on top of the other, hundreds of them at once. When a tooth wore down, the next one in the column slid up to take its place. Triceratops never ran out of teeth. Behind its eyes, a wide plate of bone flared back over its neck. Scientists call it a frill. Most horned dinosaurs had big holes in the frill to save weight. Triceratops did not. It carried the whole solid slab. For a long time people thought the frill was armor for fighting Tyrannosaurus. Many scientists now think it did another job too. It made a Triceratops easy to recognize, the way your face makes you easy to recognize.

blocks.prompt: A Case of Mistaken Identity
blocks.text: In 1887, a pair of huge horns arrived at the office of a scientist named Othniel Charles Marsh. They had been dug out of the ground near Denver, Colorado. Marsh looked them over and decided they belonged to a bison, an unusually large one that must have died fairly recently. He gave it a name and moved on. He was wrong by about sixty six million years. Two years later, a fossil hunter named John Bell Hatcher found a skull in Wyoming that made the mistake obvious. These were not bison horns. They grew from the face of an enormous reptile with a parrot's beak, a third horn on its nose, and a broad sheet of bone flaring back over its neck. Marsh named it Triceratops, which is Greek for three-horned face. For a century, everyone assumed the horns were built for fighting Tyrannosaurus rex. It is a good story, and it is partly true. Several Triceratops bones carry T. rex tooth marks. One animal had a brow horn bitten clean off, and the wound healed over afterward, which means it walked away from that fight. But the frills tell a second story. They are covered in scars, and the marks match the shape and spacing of another Triceratops's horns. These animals were fighting each other. Two of them would lock horns and shove, the way deer and elk still do today, and the frill took the damage. So the horns were not only a weapon against predators. They were also how a Triceratops settled an argument with another Triceratops.

blocks.prompt: A Face That Kept Changing
blocks.text: If you found a baby Triceratops skull and an adult Triceratops skull and set them side by side, you might not believe they came from the same animal. The baby's horns were small stubs, and they curved backward, away from its face. Its frill was short, and around the edge ran a ring of little bony triangles, like the teeth of a saw. Its whole head was round and stubby. As the animal grew, its face rebuilt itself. The brow horns straightened, then swung all the way forward until they aimed out ahead of the eyes. The nose horn pushed up. The frill stretched taller and wider, and the bony triangles around its rim flattened down and fused into it until the saw-tooth ring nearly vanished. An old Triceratops had a long, smooth, heavy face. A young one had a short, prickly, round one. Paleontologists know this because they have collected enough skulls to line the whole sequence up, from hatchling to elderly adult. The bone itself keeps the record. Under a microscope, young dinosaur bone is spongy and threaded with channels for blood vessels, because it is growing fast. Older bone is dense and tightly packed. Slice a bone, count the layers, and you can estimate how old the animal was when it died, roughly the way you can count the rings in a tree. This discovery started an argument that is still running. There is another horned dinosaur from the same rocks called Torosaurus. It looks much like Triceratops, but larger, with a longer frill carrying two big windows in it. In 2010, two paleontologists proposed something bold. Torosaurus, they said, is not a separate dinosaur at all. It is simply what a Triceratops looked like once it got very old. Other scientists disagree. They point out that some Torosaurus fossils come from animals that had not finished growing, and that plenty of clearly old Triceratops never opened those windows at all. If one turned into the other, they argue, we should have found skulls caught partway through. We have not. Both sides are looking at the same fossils, on the same shelves, in the same museums. That is worth sitting with. Fossils do not speak. Scientists read them, and reading is an argument.

notes: Triceratops horridus

About 800 teeth, always being replaced

blocks.prompt: The Last of the Horned Faces
blocks.text: Sixty six million years ago, on the flat, wet, forested plain that is now Montana and the Dakotas, the most common large animal was a Triceratops. Not one of the most common. The most. In the rock of the Hell Creek Formation, roughly two out of every five large dinosaur specimens ever collected belong to this single animal. If you could stand on that plain and look out, you would see them the way you now see cattle. It is worth being precise about what you would be looking at. An adult Triceratops ran about thirty feet long and weighed somewhere between six and twelve tons, which is to say it outweighed an African elephant, sometimes by double. Roughly a third of its length was head. Its skull, among the largest ever grown by a land animal, ended in a hooked beak, carried a horn on the nose and two above the eyes that could pass three feet, and flared backward into a sheet of bone. Most horned dinosaurs had large windows in that sheet, which saved weight. Triceratops did not. It carried the whole slab. Its mouth was an engine. Behind the beak, its teeth stood in vertical columns, three to five stacked in each, dozens of columns to a jaw. A Triceratops held something like eight hundred teeth at once and grew replacements constantly, because it wore them out constantly. Those teeth did not grind side to side the way a cow's do. They sheared past each other, top against bottom, like scissors. This animal was not browsing on soft fruit. It was cutting up the toughest plants on the floodplain. Now the interesting part, which is not the animal but the argument about it. Everyone knows what the horns were for: fighting Tyrannosaurus. The explanation is old, satisfying, and only partly supported. There is real evidence for the fights. Several Triceratops bones carry T. rex tooth marks, and at least one animal had a brow horn bitten off that then healed, meaning it survived the encounter. But when paleontologists went looking for a pattern, they found one they had not gone looking for. Triceratops frills are covered in wounds, and those wounds are far more common than on the frills of related horned dinosaurs such as Centrosaurus, whose short brow horns pointed the wrong way to lock. The damage sits precisely where another Triceratops's horns would land. The animals were fighting each other. That is how the question got better. Nobody overturned the old story by arguing louder. They counted injuries across hundreds of skulls, compared one species against another, and let the count answer. The same process is running right now over whether Torosaurus, a larger horned dinosaur with a windowed frill from the same rocks, is merely an elderly Triceratops. One team says the skulls change so profoundly with age that the two are one animal. Another says no, because some Torosaurus were still growing and some plainly old Triceratops never opened windows at all. Both teams have the same fossils on the same shelves. The disagreement is not about the bones. It is about what the bones are allowed to mean. Triceratops was there at the end. Its fossils turn up in the last few feet of rock beneath the thin grey layer of clay that marks the asteroid, the boundary where roughly three quarters of the species on Earth simply stop appearing. It is among the last non-bird dinosaurs we can find, standing in the final chapter with its shield up. It did not know it was the last of anything. It was just eating.
